topic: Does using someone's name work? (what research shows)
title: Does Hearing Your Own Name Grab Attention?
voiceover: Does hearing your own name really grab your attention? In 1959, Neville Moray ran a listening experiment where people focused on one ear and ignored the other. About a third of them noticed their own name in the ear they were ignoring. In 1995, Nicole Wood and Nelson Cowan repeated the experiment. Again, only about a third noticed their name. That means about two thirds did not notice it. In 1995, Daniel Howard and colleagues ran three experiments on names and persuasion. In them, a salesperson remembering the customer's name increased compliance with a purchase request. So your name can catch the attention of some people, and remembering a name may help persuade. Tomorrow: how can a team of smart people make a terrible decision together?

Again, only about a third noticed their name.
That means about two thirds did not notice it.
In 1995, Daniel Howard and colleagues ran three experiments on names and persuasion.
In them, a salesperson remembering the customer's name increased compliance with a purchase request.
So your name can catch the attention of some people, and remembering a name may help persuade.

description: Does your own name cut through noise? About a third of people noticed their own name in an audio channel they were told to ignore, and one set of experiments found that a salesperson remembering a name increased compliance with a purchase request. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Moray, N. (1959). Attention in dichotic listening: Affective cues and the influence of instructions. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 11(1), 56-60. Source: Wood, N., & Cowan, N. (1995). The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: How frequent are attention shifts to one's name in an irrelevant auditory channel?. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 21(1), 255-260.
accuracy_note: The 'about a third' figure is from Moray (1959) and the 1995 replication; it implies most people did not notice. The persuasion finding is from three experiments in consumer settings and is not a guarantee.
